title: Being Seen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching is that true freedom and connection come from embracing our imperfections and vulnerabilities, rather than hiding behind a mask of perfection or self-protection. By acknowledging and working with our tendency to isolate ourselves through physical sensations and self-perception, we can cultivate greater intimacy and healing in our lives. This involves reframing difficulties as opportunities for growth and transformation, rather than evidence of personal flaws, and using awareness and attention to understand and heal ourselves and our relationships.
topics: physical sensations in the face and body

sentences.text: I thought this evening I would bring up the material that I sent out on the responding gate, an email newsletter, maybe with just a little more detail, and some time for discussion.
I thought tonight we might do our small group discussion, a format to try to feel our way into what this material might actually mean for each of us.

There's a way that when we read and think about things, we're considering them in a certain way, but when we really speak to them with somebody listening, that material can be incorporated or looked at in a little different way.
Hopefully this won't be boring if you carefully read every word of that big long email and carefully studied it, but I can't imagine very many of you did.
This is a great trick of the trade that I learned from [unclear: "Norman Wichufo"]. [unclear: "Remember to access"], which is like, it's okay to repeat yourself.
It's actually probably really helpful.
Then you don't have to work so hard.
It's good for everybody.
We're cursed in our culture with the great burden of needing to be original all the time.
Not only can't you copy somebody else, you certainly can't repeat yourself.
How boring that is.
This is mostly just an email with a few extra remarks, and then we'll discuss.
I've been thinking about maybe an important part of our work.
You could say work on the cushion, or work in the practice, or just the work of being a human being.
Maybe a central part of that work that we don't always think about might be the work of just letting ourselves be seen.
Of course people do see us in a way.
They see some physicality.
We have a very complicated and subtle system of reading expressions in the body and in the face.
We see each other from the way that we speak and the ways that we move, the ways that we act, the jobs that we take.
In a way, of course, people do see us.
It also seems like a deep part of our challenge as human beings is that there's a certain way that we hide too, and that we learned how to hide as a young child and have been hiding ever since.
There's a certain desire, born out of something, to obscure, to maybe act in a certain way that we think we're supposed to act, to put on a certain kind of front for the world.
Maybe this creation of a persona is in large part a hiding that we do.
Hiding is bad too.
Letting it all hang out is good.
Hiding is bad.
I think that's not quite it either.
There's a certain way that we create a self and are always creating and recreating a self.
You could say selfing.
We're selfing all the time.
How do we do that in a way that's helpful and connecting instead of isolating and removing?
I came up with a great little phrase writing this email, that maybe the forces I wrote here, through all the forces that work within us, a kind of simulacrum of a person emerges.
We hold that between us and the world as a human shield.
Our human shield is us.
There's a lot of evidence for this being the case if you look carefully at the body and notice the sensations in the body.
In particular, notice the sensations in the face and the tensions in the face, because the face is like our social interface.
There are different psychological disorders where people can't interpret facial expressions.
We know that a vast amount of information is communicated between us just through the ways that we hold our face.
Now just take a moment and notice, even better if we lie down maybe, how does the face actually feel?
Is the jaw relaxed or is it held rigidly in some way?
Are the cheeks held in a certain way or are they relaxed?
Is there a certain expression that we're holding?
What would it be just to really let the face relax, and what would that bring up for us?
We're letting ourselves really be seen the way we actually are.
It seems kind of obvious to us that to the extent that we're hiding, there's a kind of blockage there.
There's a way that intimacy is reduced.
True intimacy and connection with others is prevented, because how can anyone be really intimate with us and really connected with us if they can't actually see who we really are?
Do we want them to be intimate with some other version of us that we're holding out to one side or in front of us?
If people can't really see us, not only is there a loss of intimacy maybe, maybe also people can't help us.
They can't really support us, and they can't really even be with us in a certain way.
We're sending a mixed message.
It really does seem like the root, or a root cause, of our existential suffering.
The Buddha expressed suffering as having three main categories.
The first is just obvious pain, physical pain, emotional pain.
Someone hurts you in some obvious way.
You feel pain, right?
So that's the first category.
We call that dukkha-dukkha, like suffering suffering.
Dukkha-dukkha, which is a good expression.
Oh, dukkha-dukkha.
Then the second kind of suffering, or dukkha, he talked about was suffering due to change.
Dukkha-haranama or something like that.
That's interesting.
He gave change a whole category.
That's worth looking at.
That could be a whole other talk or series of talks, where you could write that talk.
What does the suffering do to change?
He doesn't just mean that everything's going along fine and there's no change, then there's a change and you don't like that and then there's suffering.
He's talking more like moment by moment, moment by moment.
Everything is changing.
There's a certain kind of trouble for us because we are in a resistant relationship to that change.
He's not saying that change is inherently bad, but that there's something about our relationship to change that causes suffering, and that this is quite universal.
Then the third category of dukkha is dukkha-samskara.
Samskara is just the way the mind cognizes reality.
There's a suffering from just the way we understand existence.
That sense that even on the best of days, this little niggly sense in the background, on the best of days, or right after you've got really good news, the sense that, you know what I mean?
Something is not going on.
It's not quite something.
Not quite right.
It seems like a great underlying cause of these levels of suffering and disharmony, disease even when there's happiness.
There's a little bit of disharmony.
It's separation.
We feel separated.
We feel isolated.
I think as we practice, we notice this sense of isolation and separation from others, and sometimes even a sense of separation from people very close to us.
That's a certain kind of trouble.
Then I think as we practice, we also notice that there's a separation from ourself, which is a little more subtle, a little harder to understand.
The English language, I think, and even psychology language doesn't really, it makes it hard to put a finger on this.
The sense of an internal divide, and maybe we feel this just from the results of it, a sense of agitation or dis-ease, something able to settle on ourself.
Apparently Katagiri Roshi used to say that to practice zazen is to settle the self on the self.
To settle the self on the self.
Then he would usually say, and let the life flower bloom.
This with a funny Japanese accent, which I won't attempt to do.
This hiding, and we certainly have seen this, I think, in our lives.
Sometimes you notice something about yourself that you hadn't noticed because you somehow had not been seeing it, hiding it from yourself.

As we watch the voices and feelings and ideas and sensations that come and go, we also notice that there's a voice longing, a voice longing for connection, for healing, for being seen, for everything to be revealed.
Other voices are afraid of that, or resistant to that, or something, and are blocking that.
So I was trying to think about, well, how can we really work with this and not just have it be yet another thing that's wrong with us?
Like, oh great, one more reason why we're screwed up.
What a great religion.
What would be a way that we could work with this sense of being hidden, being obscured, that would actually be helpful?
And how could we work with that not only in our self but also in our relationships with others?
This feeling maybe that there's a wound within us that's just too big.
Maybe it's possible to let it be seen.

And so I was reflecting that it's always wise for us, and we've seen this again and again in our lives and in our practice and our study, to return to our main tools, the reliable tools in our toolbox.
They do not seem to be how smart we are or how skilled we are or trying to be a good person.
It seems like the reliable tools in our toolbox for this kind of work are awareness and attention.
